target_customer: Individuals and prosumers first, then teams and businesses paying for storage and collaboration
problem: People carried files on USB sticks or emailed themselves; existing backup and sync tools were heavyweight and did not just work across machines.
business_model: freemium subscription with referral-driven growth, paid storage tiers and team plans

founders.name: Drew Houston
education: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, computer science degree (Wikipedia)
previous_startups: SAT prep company co-founded during college, outcome not stated (Wikipedia)
founders.background_notes: Co-founded Dropbox in 2007 per the YC page; met Ferdowsi at MIT (Wikipedia).

founders.name: Arash Ferdowsi
education: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, electrical engineering and computer science, dropped out in his last semester (Wikipedia)
founders.background_notes: Listed as a founder on the YC company page.

technical_complexity.rationale: Reliable cross-platform file sync with delta transfers and filesystem hooks on Windows, Mac and Linux was hard to get right at the time.

defensibility.rationale: Sync was copyable and Microsoft and Google later bundled rivals, but reliability, habit and sharing created stickiness.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Microsoft, Google and Apple shipped free substitutes; Dropbox still IPO'd in 2018 but growth slowed and it cut staff in 2023 and 2024.

market_need_then: YC application argued existing tools were heavyweight; Dropbox's 2007 demo drew strong interest from developers and the press.

branding.name_origin: Dropbox was a term the founders used when getting together to play computer games, per one account; the first idea was Folder Anywhere.
branding.domain_note: Launched on getdropbox.com because dropbox.com was taken; bought dropbox.com in October 2009, reportedly for $300,000
branding.brand_signature: The open box icon and the free space referral program

rebrands.why: Company renamed and bought the exact match domain

branding.community_and_virality: Domain upgrade covered by TechCrunch and domain press; referral program details not confirmed by this run's sources.

brand_strength.rationale: The name became a generic verb for file sharing among consumers; evidence from coverage, though logo and referral details were not retrieved.

outcome_analysis: Dropbox solved file sync better than 2007 incumbents and grew through word of mouth, raising a $250M round at a reported $4B in 2011 and going public in March 2018. Free substitutes from big platforms and macro headwinds slowed growth; it cut about 16% of staff in 2023 and about 20% in October 2024. Rivals recorded here rather than as competition at founding: Mozy and Carbonite (online backup), Box.net, and Microsoft SkyDrive, Groove and FolderShare, whose only sources found are retrospective pages dated years after the 2007 batch.
notes: Series A: TechCrunch (2009-11-24) headline says $6M Sequoia-led Series A in October 2008 and states that Accel did participate; GigaOm's $7.25M was denied by Houston. Series A valuation of $25M and the seed valuation of $5M come only from Global Venturing (Vator gives $29.3M), TechCrunch gives none. Seed was $1.2M of convertible debt led by Sequoia with Amidzad Partners (TechCrunch); the date is not stated there, so 2007 follows Global Venturing. Series B on 2011-10-18 was led by Index Ventures per TechCrunch, which does not state the valuation; the $4B is a prior report cited there and by Global Venturing. IPO on Nasdaq 2018-03-23 per Global Venturing. YC listing says founded 2008, other sources say 2007. Layoffs: 2023 16 percent (500 roles) and Oct 2024 20 percent (528), a 2021 cut appears in one outlet only. Founder education is from the Wikipedia pages on each founder; no prior employers are stated there. Competitors removed because the sources found are retrospective and dated years after founding. Referral program and logo not sourced this run.
